> whose functions called here are trivial, and are guaranteed to be inlined

While the performance improvement is likely to be fairly small, it likely won't be zero. I would have thought that any improvement would still be worth taking. Wasted cycles consume time and given that these forms of waste are littered throughout the entire codebase, there is no harm in taking easy wins when they require almost no effort to achieve.

>An optimizing compiler should be able to reduce RAM fetches, and assign registers to values appropriately to optimize the code for us.

As I alluded in the original comment, I've checked the assembly and the newer version has fewer memory accesses. The "sufficiently smart compiler" is often invoked but the reality doesn't often hold up.

MSVC with optimisations:

Before, the size is read for both `is_empty` and `size`

```
171: 	if (p_cstr.is_empty()) {
mov         rcx,qword ptr [rdx+8] 

179: 	const char *end = src + p_cstr.size();
 mov         rdi,qword ptr [rdi+8] 
```

After, the size is stored in `rdi` for the entire call and no more memory accesses are needed.

```
   171: 	const uint64_t p_cstr_size = p_cstr.size();
 mov         rdi,qword ptr [rdx+8]  
```

There are four fewer calls to `mov` with this change.

> Wasted cycles consume time and given that these forms of waste are littered throughout the entire codebase

That is certainly true! We have a lot of areas that are in dire need of improvement :)

> there is no harm in taking easy wins when they require almost no effort to achieve.

It's always important to weigh optimization against other concerns - readability, maintainability, code churn, and robustness, to name a few. That's why it's important to show a practical improvement over the previous code, especially with micro-optimizations! In a big codebase like this, there rarely are any 'easy wins'.

> As I alluded in the original comment, I've checked the assembly and the newer version has fewer memory accesses. The "sufficiently smart compiler" is often invoked but the reality doesn't often hold up.
> [...]
> There are four fewer calls to `mov` with this change.

Interesting look! I really thought the compiler should have been able to cache the variable. I think this may be an MSVC thing - compared to gcc and clang, it's very bad at things like this.

Anyway, four instructions is not _nothing_ — but it's also not a lot. Considering the rest of the overhead (from this function and callers), I doubt you'd be able to measure a practical improvement in a benchmark (especially if cache misses are involved).

I realize I'm being very critical right now - sorry! Your attention is still very much appreciated :)
If you're interested in meaningfully improving the engine's performance, I highly recommend whipping up a profiler and taking a look at functions that pop up near the top. I think you'll quickly find something that is worthy of attention :)
